$comment: Doodles type direction. Fonts come from foundations/typography/source/pairings.json plus the newPairings below; this file says which suit this approach and how to set them. Unlike Humanist Minimal, Doodles allows a hand-lettered display, under strict limits. Sizes are rules of thumb unless a source is given.
character: Two hands on one page: a hand-lettered headline that sounds like someone talking, and plain, clear set type for everything you need to read or act on. The lettering joins the drawing; the body type stays out of it.

anatomy.$comment: What to look for when judging type for this approach.

strokes.want: Monoline, like a felt-tip or marker
strokes.why: Matches the one-pen rule; a brush or nib swell reads as a different tool.

forms.want: Print (unjoined) letters, open counters, slightly irregular
forms.why: Readable at a glance; joined scripts slow reading and look formal.

variation.want: Some glyph variation (alternates or a 'bounce' axis)
variation.why: Repeated identical letters give away a font; variation keeps the hand alive.

weight.want: Bold enough that stems are 1.5-3x the pen width
weight.why: Lettering sits on top of the marks in the hierarchy.

apertures.why: Body text sits near busy marks; open letters stay legible.

tone.want: Friendly, plain sans (or a calm serif for long reading)
tone.why: Lets the drawing carry the personality.

avoid: Joke or 'comic' fonts with no text weight
Hand fonts for body text, buttons or prices
Two different hand faces in one piece

fit.$comment: core = recommended, good = works, accent = special cases, avoid = not for this approach.

bricolage-figtree.why: The irregular, ink-trapped display reads as hand-touched next to doodles, and Figtree stays clear for body. The best choice when the headline is set rather than lettered.

nunito.why: Round terminals echo the round pen ends; keep doodles grown-up (no faces overload), because round type plus doodles drifts towards childish.

young-onest.why: The soft, heavy serif looks inked with a felt-tip and holds its own against a wall; Onest is a clear body.

schibsted.why: Neutral grotesque gives the clean-type-plus-scribbles contrast; works when the doodles carry all the warmth.

source.why: Very readable for sketchnote pages with real text; the serif display is calm next to busy marks.

fraunces-commissioner.why: Its own bouncy charm competes with the doodles; use SOFT high, WONK off, one weight, margin mode only.

alegreya.why: Broad-nib calligraphic contrast is a second 'hand' that clashes with the monoline pen; fine for literary pieces with few marks.

instrument.why: High-contrast condensed serif with margin doodles makes an editorial-notebook look; avoid in wall mode, where its hairlines get lost.

plex.why: Engineered tone suits whiteboard-style technical sketchnotes; otherwise too cool for the style.

newPairings.name: Marker Talk
newPairings.mood: A marker hand that is designed to be read: monoline, unjoined, with Bounce and Informality axes that make repeated letters vary. Figtree keeps body text calm.
newPairings.bestFor: Doodles headlines, labels and annotations; social posts, posters, playful landing pages.

display.style: Marker-style handwriting sans with bounce and informality axes
display.designer: Shantell Martin, Arrow Type (Stephen Nixon), Anya Danilova
display.notes: A marker-style font based on the artwork, handwriting and creative philosophy of artist Shantell Martin, built for typographic play and animation (Arrow Type README). Use BNCE 30-60 and INFM 50-100 for headlines (needs the rlig feature on for randomisation); INFM 0 for labels at small sizes. On Google Fonts since 2023.

newPairings.name: Notebook Hand
newPairings.mood: A quick, teenage-notebook marker hand over a warm humanist sans from the same designer, so the two share proportions.
newPairings.bestFor: Sketchnote pages, menus, education, friendly local brands.

display.notes: Single weight; described by its designer as an interpretation of a teenager's handwriting. On Google Fonts since 2011. Headlines and labels only.

handLettering.$comment: Rules for any hand lettering, drawn or from a hand-lettered font.
where: Labels and annotations of up to 3 words
One emphasised word inside a set headline
handLettering.drawnByHand: For hero pieces, letter the headline by hand with the piece's pen (stems 1.5-3 pen widths, so use a marker or double-stroke the fineliner), then vectorise. Keep the font for everyday work.
handLettering.baseline: May bounce (Shantell BNCE) or drift by up to 4% of the cap height; set type never does.
handLettering.mixing: Hand display + set body. Never two hand faces, never a hand face plus a drawn headline in the same piece.

typeWithArt.weightMatch: Hand-lettered headline stems at 1.5-3x the pen width, so the words sit one step above the marks. Set body text weight close to the pen width.
typeWithArt.scaleMatch: Headline cap height at least 1.5x the height of the average surrounding mark, so the words win over the doodles.
typeWithArt.alignment: Set text aligned to one edge. Hand lettering can tilt and sit freely, but stays on or next to a clearing.
typeWithArt.spacing: A mark-free band of at least one margin around body text and the CTA; marks may touch the headline only to point at or underline it.

sizes.$comment: Headline cap height as a share of the canvas height, and body text minimums. Rules of thumb. Hand faces have small x-heights at the same size, so they run 10-15% larger than Humanist Minimal's headlines.
sizes.viewingDistance: Sign-industry rule of thumb: about 1 inch (25 mm) of letter height for every 10 feet (3 m) of viewing distance for basic legibility; double it for comfortable reading, and add 15% for hand faces.

measure.source: Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style

setting.case: Sentence case everywhere, in lettering too. Capitals only for set labels of one to three words.
setting.rag: Ragged right; no justified text; balance headline lines (text-wrap: balance).
setting.numbers: Prices, dates and times are set in the body or mono face, never hand-lettered; a doodle may circle or point to them.

rules: Hand lettering for up to 8 headline words or 3-word labels; set type for everything else.
One hand face (or drawn lettering) per piece, never both.
Three sizes and two weights per piece; sentence case.
Body text and CTA on plain ground with a mark-free band around them.
No joined scripts, joke fonts or grunge textures.
